raw_case_text:
A 59-year-old male patient had low back pain without obvious cause for nearly one year, which was aggravated during activities, accompanied by intermittent fever, night sweat, and fatigue. He presented to a local tuberculosis hospital with a suspicion of "lumbar tuberculosis" and was given anti-tuberculosis treatment: isoniazide 300 mg (po qd), rifampicin 450 mg (po qd), ethambutol 750 mg (po qd), streptomycin 750 mg (im qd). At this time, Mycobacterium susceptibility test showed sensitivity to all types of anti-TB drugs. The patient continued to have low back pain. For further treatment, he visited the orthopedics outpatient of our hospital, we considered lumbar tuberculosis, and recommended surgical treatment. This patient contracted HIV five years ago from homosexual intercourse. Early screening blood viral load is 129,800 copies/mL, then began to receive antiviral treatment (ART): lamivudine/tenofovir/efavirenz, drug regimen did not change in five years. The blood viral load dropped to undetectable levels 10 months after ART and remained at this level at annual viral load screening. CD4+T lymphocyte count fluctuated between 200-300 cells /ul.
On physical examination, the patient had a limp gait with tenderness and percussion in the spinous processes of lumbar 1-3 and paravertebral regions, without radiation to the lower limbs. The muscle strength of each muscle group of both lower limbs was grade 5. The active and passive movements of the lumbar spine were obviously limited. The active range of motion of the lumbar spine: forward flexion (10 ), backward extension (20 ), left flexion (10 ), right flexion (20 ), left rotation (10 ), right rotation (20 ). Bilateral straight leg raising test and strengthening test were negative, bilateral femoral nerve pull test was negative, bilateral knee tendon reflex and Achilles tendon reflex were normal, and bilateral Babinski sign was negative. Laboratory tests were as follows: C-reactive protein 11.9mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 38.00mm/h, CD4+T lymphocyte count 219 cells /ul, and albumin 33.0g/L.
Preoperative lumbar X-ray showed uneven density and narrowing of the L2/3 intervertebral space (Figure 1A and B). Lumbar CT and enhanced MRI showed cavities and osteolytic destruction in L2/3 with multiple irregular sequestrum, the paravertebral abscess was large and prominent. Subsequently, the patient underwent lumbar focus debridement, decompression, internal fixation, and bone graft fusion under general anesthesia (Figure 1C-H). The operation was successful, anti-tuberculosis and anti-viral therapy was continued after the operation. The X-ray reexamination on the third day after operation showed that the internal fixation was firm and the position of the fusion cage was satisfactory. (Figure 2) He was discharged 20 days later.
Four months after operation, the patient was found that the incision scar was swollen, with ulceration and pus (Figure 3), and was hospitalized again. Physical examination revealed a 15cm long longitudinal surgical scar in the middle of the waist, with a 1mm diameter tear at the lower end of it, yellowish green pus flowed out around the extrusion. The reexamination showed the formation of bilateral psoas abscess, central liquefaction necrosis, abnormal soft tissue density shadow under the lower back, considering inflammatory lesions, and local sinus formation. (Figure 4) After discussion with the general practitioner, the patient could be treated with ultrasound-guided puncture and drainage of pus (Figure 5), followed by surgical evacuation.
All the operations were successful. After regular dressing change and observation of the incision, the wound healed smoothly and the patient was discharged. During the follow-up, it was learned that the patient was resistant to rifampin and isoniazid in the tuberculosis drug resistance test in the local hospital, and he was advised to change to oral rifapentine and prothionamide. So far, he has not relapsed and is living well.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old HIV-positive male presented to the orthopedics outpatient clinic with a 1-year history of progressive activity-aggravated low back pain, intermittent fever, night sweats, and fatigue.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed insidious-onset low back pain nearly 1 year prior to presentation that worsened with physical activity and was accompanied by intermittent fever, night sweats, and fatigue. He had been diagnosed at a local tuberculosis hospital with lumbar tuberculosis (with initial pan-susceptible Mycobacterium drug susceptibility testing) and treated with oral isoniazid 300 mg daily, rifampicin 450 mg daily, ethambutol 750 mg daily, and intramuscular streptomycin 750 mg daily, but his low back pain persisted, prompting orthopedic referral. Four months after lumbar surgery, he was readmitted with swelling, ulceration, and purulent discharge from his lumbar surgical scar.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with HIV infection 5 years prior (acquired via homosexual intercourse; baseline viral load 129,800 copies/mL), stably maintained on lamivudine/tenofovir/efavirenz for 5 years with undetectable viral load achieved 10 months after ART initiation and CD4+ counts fluctuating between 200 and 300 cells/µL.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic low back pain, intermittent fever, night sweats, and fatigue; negative for lower extremity radicular pain. Home medications: lamivudine, tenofovir, efavirenz, isoniazid 300 mg qd, rifampicin 450 mg qd, ethambutol 750 mg qd, and streptomycin 750 mg IM qd.

objective.physical_examination: Initial examination showed an antalgic (limp) gait, spinous process and paravertebral tenderness and percussion pain at L1–L3 without radiation to the lower extremities, and severely restricted lumbar active range of motion (forward flexion 10°, extension 20°, left lateral flexion 10°, right lateral flexion 20°, left rotation 10°, right rotation 20°). Lower extremity motor strength was 5/5 throughout, knee and Achilles reflexes were normal, and bilateral straight-leg raise, femoral nerve stretch, and Babinski signs were negative. At 4-month readmission, examination revealed a 15 cm longitudinal midline lumbar surgical scar with a 1 mm lower-pole dehiscence extruding yellowish-green pus.
objective.routine_investigations: Preoperative laboratory tests showed CRP 11.9 mg/L, ESR 38.00 mm/h, and serum albumin 33.0 g/L. Preoperative lumbar spine radiographs demonstrated narrowing and uneven density of the L2/L3 intervertebral disc space.
objective.advanced_workup: Preoperative CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 219 cells/µL. Lumbar CT and contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated L2/L3 vertebral cavities and osteolytic destruction with multiple irregular sequestra and a large paravertebral abscess. At 4-month readmission, repeat lumbar imaging revealed bilateral psoas abscesses with central liquefactive necrosis, subcutaneous inflammatory soft-tissue changes, and a local sinus tract.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Multidrug-resistant lumbar spinal tuberculosis (L2/L3 spondylodiscitis and recurrent bilateral psoas abscesses) in a 59-year-old male with virologically suppressed HIV infection (undetectable HIV viral load on lamivudine/tenofovir/efavirenz, CD4 count 219 cells/µL). Initial surgical management consisted of lumbar focus debridement, decompression, internal fixation, and bone graft fusion with continuation of first-line anti-TB therapy and ART. Following readmission at 4 months for recurrent bilateral psoas abscesses and sinus tract formation, he underwent ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage followed by open surgical evacuation and regular wound care. Subsequent local hospital mycobacterial drug susceptibility testing identified acquired resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid, prompting substitution with oral rifapentine and prothionamide, resulting in complete wound healing and sustained relapse-free survival.
